Go Syntax.aiRubric: Check logic, syntax, and output for Go Syntax.

lessons.title: Hello Go
lessons.theory:
## A Modern Language for the Cloud
Go (or Golang) was created at Google in 2009 by the original inventors of C and Unix. They were frustrated by how slow massive C++ codebases took to compile, and how difficult it was to write concurrent (multi-threaded) code in languages like Java or Python.

Go was designed to be incredibly fast to compile, highly performant (it compiles directly to machine code, no JVM required), and exceptionally good at handling thousands of simultaneous connections. It has strict formatting (there is only one way to format Go code, enforced by `gofmt`) and a tiny, minimalist syntax.

Because of its speed, low memory footprint, and native concurrency, Go became the language of the cloud. Kubernetes, Docker, Terraform, and Prometheus are all written entirely in Go.
lessons.instructions:
## Task: Your First Go Program
1. Write a Go program that prints a greeting
2. The package must be `main`
3. Use `fmt.Println` to output "Hello from Go!"

lessons.rubric: Code matches Go structure and prints 'Hello from Go!'

lessons.title: Variables & Types
lessons.theory:
## Strong and Static
Go is a statically typed language, meaning the type of a variable (integer, string, boolean) is checked at compile time, catching errors before the code even runs.

However, Go offers a 'short variable declaration' syntax (`:=`) that makes it feel as lightweight as a dynamic language like Python. 

```go
// Explicit typing
var name string = "Alice"
var age int = 25

// Short declaration (Go infers the type)
country := "Canada"
score := 99.5
```
Go is extremely strict about unused variables. If you declare a variable but never use it, the Go compiler will flat-out refuse to compile the program. This keeps Go codebases clean and free of dead code.
lessons.instructions:
## Task: Declare Variables
1. Declare `year` as an int using explicit typing
2. Declare `language` as a string using type inference (`var`)
3. Declare `version` as a float using short declaration (`:=`)
4. Print them all
lessons.starterCode:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    ___ year ___ = 2024
    ___ language = "Go"
    version ___ 1.22
    
    fmt.Printf("Year: %d, Language: %s, Version: %.2f
", year, language, version)
}
lessons.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    var year int = 2024
    var language = "Go"
    version := 1.22
    
    fmt.Printf("Year: %d, Language: %s, Version: %.2f
", year, language, version)
}
lessons.hint: var name type. var name = value. name := value.
lessons.rubric: All three variable types declared correctly and printed.

Goroutines.aiRubric: Check logic, syntax, and output for Goroutines.

lessons.title: Goroutines Basics
lessons.theory:
## Ultra-Lightweight Threads
The crown jewel of Go is its concurrency model: **Goroutines**.

In languages like Java or Python, creating an operating system thread is 'heavy'—it takes 1-2 megabytes of RAM. You can only run a few thousand threads before crashing the server. 

A Goroutine is a virtual thread managed by the Go runtime, not the OS. It starts with just 2 kilobytes of RAM. You can easily spawn 100,000 goroutines on a basic laptop.

To run a function concurrently in the background, you literally just add the word `go` in front of it:
```go
go sendEmail(user)
go processImage(image)
```
The Go scheduler automatically maps these hundreds of thousands of goroutines onto your physical CPU cores, making highly concurrent web servers trivial to write.
lessons.instructions:
## Task: Start Goroutines

2. Call it once normally, and once as a goroutine
3. Simulate a small delay with `time.Sleep` in the loop

lessons.title: Channels
lessons.theory:
## Communication Between Goroutines
When you have thousands of goroutines running simultaneously, they eventually need to share data. Traditional languages use shared memory and 'Locks' (Mutexes) to prevent data corruption, which is notoriously difficult to program correctly without causing deadlocks.

Go encourages a different philosophy: *"Do not communicate by sharing memory; instead, share memory by communicating."*

Go uses **Channels**—think of them as safe, typed conveyor belts between goroutines. One goroutine can send data into the channel, and another goroutine can read data out of it. The channel handles all the locking and synchronization under the hood, making concurrent programming safe and intuitive.
```go
messages := make(chan string)
go func() { messages <- "ping" }()  // Send into channel
msg := <-messages                   // Receive from channel
```
lessons.instructions:
## Task: Channel Sender & Receiver

2. Start a goroutine that sends 3 messages to the channel
3. Receive and print the 3 messages in main
lessons.hint: make(chan type). ch <- val sends. val := <-ch receives.
lessons.rubric: Channel created. Messages sent with <- and received with <-. Prints Ping Pong Done.

Go Web Servers.aiRubric: Check logic, syntax, and output for Go Web Servers.

lessons.title: net/http
lessons.theory:
## The Standard Library Web Server
In Python, you need a framework like Django or FastAPI, plus an application server like Gunicorn, to run a production web server. In Node.js, you need Express.

Go's standard library includes the `net/http` package, which is so robust and performant that you can use it directly in production without any third-party frameworks.

```go
http.HandleFunc("/hello", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    fmt.Fprintf(w, "Hello, World!")
})
http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil)
```
This tiny snippet starts a high-performance web server. Because every incoming HTTP request automatically runs in its own lightweight Goroutine, this server can handle tens of thousands of simultaneous connections right out of the box.

lessons.rubric: Go pseudocode correctly defines a basic net/http handler.

Docker Containers.aiRubric: Check logic, syntax, and output for Docker Containers.

lessons.title: What is Docker?
lessons.theory:
## The Shipping Container for Code
Before Docker, deploying software was a nightmare. Code that worked perfectly on a developer's Mac would crash on the Linux production server because of different OS versions, missing dependencies, or conflicting Python libraries. This was the classic *"It works on my machine"* problem.

Docker solved this by introducing **Containers**. A container packages the code, the runtime, the system tools, and the exact libraries into a single, standardized box. 

Think of the global shipping industry. Before standard shipping containers, loading a boat with cars, barrels, and sacks of grain was slow and custom. Standard steel containers meant ships, cranes, and trucks only had to handle one shape. Docker does this for software. If your app runs in a Docker container on your laptop, it is mathematically guaranteed to run exactly the same way on AWS, Google Cloud, or your coworker's machine.
lessons.instructions:
## Task: Docker Commands

2. Include: build, run, ps, stop, rmi

lessons.title: Writing a Dockerfile
lessons.theory:
## The Blueprint
To create a Docker container, you write a text file called a **Dockerfile**. It acts as a step-by-step recipe for building your application's environment.

```dockerfile
# 1. Start from a lightweight Linux image with Go installed
FROM golang:1.21-alpine

# 2. Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# 3. Copy your code into the container
COPY . .

# 4. Compile the Go application
RUN go build -o myapi

# 5. Define what runs when the container starts
CMD ["./myapi"]
```
When you run `docker build`, Docker reads this file, executes the steps, and takes a snapshot. This snapshot is called an **Image**. You can then push this image to a registry (like Docker Hub) and pull it onto any server in the world to run it instantly.
lessons.instructions:
## Task: Node.js Dockerfile
1. Write the text of a Dockerfile for a Node.js app
2. Use `node:18-alpine` as base
3. Copy package.json, run `npm install`, copy code, run `npm start`
lessons.starterCode:
dockerfile = """
___ node:18-alpine

___ /usr/src/app

___ package*.json ./

___ npm install

___ . .

___ ["npm", "start"]
"""

print("Your Dockerfile:")
print(dockerfile)
lessons.solution:
dockerfile = """
FROM node:18-alpine

WORKDIR /usr/src/app

COPY package*.json ./

RUN npm install

COPY . .

CMD ["npm", "start"]
"""

print("Your Dockerfile:")
print(dockerfile)
lessons.hint: FROM sets base. WORKDIR sets dir. COPY moves files. RUN executes in build. CMD is startup.
lessons.rubric: Valid Node.js Dockerfile using standard keywords.

Kubernetes Basics.aiRubric: Check logic, syntax, and output for Kubernetes Basics.

lessons.title: Orchestrating Containers
lessons.theory:
## The Need for Kubernetes
Docker is perfect for running 1 or 2 containers on a single server. But what if you are a massive bank with 5,000 containers spread across 500 different servers?

If a server catches fire, who notices and restarts those 100 containers on a healthy server? How do you route internet traffic to them? How do you upgrade them without downtime? Doing this manually is impossible.

This is where **Kubernetes (K8s)** comes in. Kubernetes is a Container Orchestrator. You give Kubernetes a cluster of servers, and you declare your desired state: *"I want 5 copies of the Login API running at all times."* Kubernetes automatically schedules the containers onto the servers, monitors their health, restarts them if they crash, and manages the network load balancing between them. It acts as the intelligent operating system for your entire data center.

gRPC.aiRubric: Check logic, syntax, and output for gRPC.

lessons.title: High-Speed APIs
lessons.theory:
## gRPC vs REST
Most web APIs use REST, sending data back and forth as JSON strings over HTTP/1.1. While JSON is easy for humans to read, it is slow to parse and takes up a lot of bandwidth, which becomes a bottleneck when hundreds of microservices are talking to each other internally.

**gRPC** (developed by Google) is a high-speed alternative designed for internal microservice communication. Instead of JSON, it uses **Protocol Buffers (Protobuf)**, which serializes data into a highly compressed, binary format. 

Furthermore, gRPC runs on HTTP/2, allowing multiple requests to be multiplexed over a single connection simultaneously. An internal gRPC API written in Go can be 10x faster and use a fraction of the CPU compared to a standard JSON REST API.
lessons.instructions:
## Task: Protobuf vs JSON Size
1. Compare the string length of a JSON object vs a mock Binary representation.
2. Print the difference in size.
lessons.starterCode:
import json

data = {"id": 104, "name": "Alice", "active": True}

# Standard REST JSON string
json_string = json.___(data)
json_size = len(json_string)

# Mock gRPC Protobuf binary (usually much smaller, just the raw data packed)
mock_binary_string = "104Alice1"
binary_size = len(___)

print(f"JSON Size: {json_size} bytes")
print(f"Protobuf Size: {binary_size} bytes")
print(f"gRPC is {json_size - binary_size} bytes smaller!")
lessons.solution:
import json

data = {"id": 104, "name": "Alice", "active": True}

# Standard REST JSON string
json_string = json.dumps(data)
json_size = len(json_string)

# Mock gRPC Protobuf binary (usually much smaller, just the raw data packed)
mock_binary_string = "104Alice1"
binary_size = len(mock_binary_string)

print(f"JSON Size: {json_size} bytes")
print(f"Protobuf Size: {binary_size} bytes")
print(f"gRPC is {json_size - binary_size} bytes smaller!")
lessons.hint: Use json.dumps(). Check length of mock_binary_string.
lessons.rubric: Shows JSON is larger (around 40 bytes) compared to the mock binary (9 bytes).

Service Meshes.aiRubric: Check logic, syntax, and output for Service Meshes.

lessons.title: Managing Microservices
lessons.theory:
## The Service Mesh
As a company transitions from one monolithic application to 100 tiny microservices, new problems arise. How do these services securely authenticate with each other? How do you trace a request that bounces through 5 different services to find out which one is slow? How do you implement retry logic if a network hiccup occurs?

Writing this complex networking and security logic directly into every microservice is a massive anti-pattern. 

Instead, Cloud Native architectures use a **Service Mesh** (like Istio or Linkerd). A Service Mesh injects a tiny network proxy (a sidecar) next to every single container. The microservice doesn't talk to the network directly; it talks to the proxy. The proxies handle all the mutual TLS encryption, retries, load balancing, and tracing completely transparently, allowing the developers to focus purely on business logic.
lessons.instructions:
## Task: Sidecar Simulator
1. Simulate a request going through a sidecar proxy.
2. The proxy should intercept the request, encrypt it, and pass it to the destination.
lessons.starterCode:
class SidecarProxy:
    def __init__(self, service_name):
        self.service_name = service_name
        
    def send(self, destination, data):
        print(f"[{self.service_name} Proxy] Encrypting data...")
        encrypted = f"**{data}**"
        print(f"[{self.service_name} Proxy] Sending to {destination.service_name} Proxy...")
        destination.___(encrypted)
        
    def receive(self, data):
        print(f"[{self.service_name} Proxy] Decrypting data...")
        decrypted = data.replace('*', '')
        print(f"[{self.service_name} App] Received: {decrypted}")

app_a = SidecarProxy("Service_A")
app_b = SidecarProxy("Service_B")

app_a.___(app_b, "Hello Microservice!")
lessons.solution:
class SidecarProxy:
    def __init__(self, service_name):
        self.service_name = service_name
        
    def send(self, destination, data):
        print(f"[{self.service_name} Proxy] Encrypting data...")
        encrypted = f"**{data}**"
        print(f"[{self.service_name} Proxy] Sending to {destination.service_name} Proxy...")
        destination.receive(encrypted)
        
    def receive(self, data):
        print(f"[{self.service_name} Proxy] Decrypting data...")
        decrypted = data.replace('*', '')
        print(f"[{self.service_name} App] Received: {decrypted}")

app_a = SidecarProxy("Service_A")
app_b = SidecarProxy("Service_B")

app_a.send(app_b, "Hello Microservice!")
lessons.hint: destination.receive(encrypted) and app_a.send(app_b, ...)
lessons.rubric: Data successfully routes A Proxy -> B Proxy -> B App.

Cloud Operators.aiRubric: Check logic, syntax, and output for Cloud Operators.

lessons.title: K8s Operators
lessons.theory:
## Automating Human Tasks
Kubernetes is great at managing stateless web servers. But databases are difficult. If a database goes down, you can't just restart it randomly; you have to run backups, elect a new master node, and sync data. Historically, this required a human database administrator.

The **Operator Pattern** solves this. An Operator is a custom piece of software (usually written in Go) that runs inside Kubernetes. It acts as a robot administrator that understands the specific operational rules of a complex application.

For example, if you install a PostgreSQL Operator, you can tell Kubernetes *"Give me a 3-node Postgres cluster."* The Operator takes over, automatically provisioning the disks, starting the nodes, configuring replication, and watching for failures 24/7, effectively automating the human administrator's job.
lessons.instructions:
## Task: Operator Loop
1. An operator constantly runs a 'Reconciliation Loop'.
2. It checks the 'Desired State' against the 'Current State'.
3. Simulate an operator checking if a database has a backup.
lessons.starterCode:
def reconcile_loop(current_state, desired_state):
    print("--- Reconciliation Loop Running ---")
    
    if current_state['needs_backup'] != desired_state['___']:
        print("[Operator Action] Taking database backup to match desired state...")
        current_state['___'] = desired_state['___']
        return "Action Taken"
    
    return "No Action Needed"

desired = {'needs_backup': False} # We don't want it to NEED a backup, we want it DONE
current = {'needs_backup': True}

print(reconcile_loop(current, desired))
# Loop runs again later
print(reconcile_loop(current, desired))
lessons.solution:
def reconcile_loop(current_state, desired_state):
    print("--- Reconciliation Loop Running ---")
    
    if current_state['needs_backup'] != desired_state['needs_backup']:
        print("[Operator Action] Taking database backup to match desired state...")
        current_state['needs_backup'] = desired_state['needs_backup']
        return "Action Taken"
    
    return "No Action Needed"

desired = {'needs_backup': False} # We don't want it to NEED a backup, we want it DONE
current = {'needs_backup': True}

print(reconcile_loop(current, desired))
# Loop runs again later
print(reconcile_loop(current, desired))
lessons.hint: Key is 'needs_backup'.
lessons.rubric: First loop takes action, second loop takes no action.

lessons.title: Go Mod Init
lessons.theory:
## Dependency Management
In the early days, Go didn't have a built-in package manager like NPM for Node or Pip for Python. Code was pulled directly from the `GOPATH`, which caused massive headaches with versioning.

Go Modules solved this. To start a new project, you run `go mod init github.com/yourname/project`. This creates a `go.mod` file, similar to a `package.json`. 

When you import a third-party library in your code and run `go build`, Go automatically downloads the library and records the exact cryptographic version hash in a `go.sum` file. This guarantees that if another developer clones your repository a year later, they will download the exact same versions of the dependencies, ensuring repeatable and deterministic builds.
lessons.instructions:
## Task: Init a Module

lessons.starterCode: go ___ ___ github.com/mabel/app
lessons.solution: go mod init github.com/mabel/app
lessons.hint: Use mod init
lessons.rubric: Correctly constructs the go mod init command.

lessons.title: Channel Basics
lessons.theory:
## Unbuffered vs Buffered
When a goroutine sends data into an **Unbuffered Channel** (`make(chan int)`), it immediately blocks and freezes until another goroutine pulls the data out of the channel. This guarantees perfect synchronization between the two threads.

A **Buffered Channel** (`make(chan int, 5)`) has internal capacity. A goroutine can send up to 5 items into the channel without freezing. It only blocks when it tries to send a 6th item and the buffer is full.

Buffered channels are frequently used for rate limiting and worker pools. For example, if you have 100 image processing jobs but only want to process 5 at a time to avoid crashing the server, you push the jobs into a channel buffered to 5. The worker goroutines pull jobs out, ensuring the system never exceeds its capacity.
lessons.instructions:
## Task: Send and Receive
Create a channel of integers, send the number 42 into it, and receive it.
lessons.hint: Use make(chan int) and the <- operator
lessons.rubric: Correctly uses make(chan int) and the send/receive operators.

lessons.title: The Select Statement
lessons.theory:
## Handling Multiple Channels
Often, a goroutine needs to listen to multiple channels at the same time. For example, a web server might be waiting for a database query to return on `dbChannel`, but also waiting on a `timeoutChannel` in case the query takes too long.

In Go, you use the `select` statement. It looks like a `switch` statement, but it specifically waits on channel operations.

```go
select {
case result := <-dbChannel:
    fmt.Println("Database returned:", result)
case <-time.After(2 * time.Second): // Creates a timeout channel
    fmt.Println("Timeout! Database is too slow.")
}
```
The `select` block will pause the goroutine until *one* of the cases is ready to proceed. If the database takes longer than 2 seconds, the timeout case fires, allowing the server to return an error to the user rather than freezing indefinitely.
lessons.instructions:
## Task: Select on Two Channels
Write a select statement that waits for a message from `ch1` or `ch2`.
lessons.hint: Use <- operator and case keyword
lessons.rubric: Correctly uses the case keyword and receive operator.

lessons.title: The Package Manager
lessons.theory:
## Helm: The Package Manager for Kubernetes
Writing raw Kubernetes YAML files by hand is tedious. A complex application might require 10 different YAML files for deployments, services, secrets, and volumes. 

**Helm** is the package manager for Kubernetes (think `apt` or `brew`, but for cloud infrastructure). Helm packages multiple YAML templates into a single bundle called a **Chart**.

If you want to install a complex monitoring stack like Prometheus, instead of writing thousands of lines of YAML yourself, you simply run `helm install prometheus prometheus-community/prometheus`. Helm pulls the chart from the internet, fills in the required configuration variables, and deploys all the necessary Kubernetes resources automatically.
lessons.instructions:
## Task: Install a Chart
Write the helm command to install a chart named 'my-redis' from the bitnami repository.
lessons.starterCode: helm ___ my-redis bitnami/___
lessons.solution: helm install my-redis bitnami/redis
lessons.hint: Use install and redis
lessons.rubric: Correctly uses the helm install command.

lessons.title: Values injected in Templates
lessons.theory:
## Helm Templates and Values
The true power of Helm Charts is that the YAML files are templated. 

If you have a testing environment and a production environment, you don't want to copy and paste your Kubernetes YAML files. Instead, you write one Helm Chart using placeholders. 

```yaml
# deployment.yaml
replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
```
You then provide a separate `values.yaml` file for each environment. For staging, your values file sets `replicaCount: 1`. For production, the values file sets `replicaCount: 5`. When Helm installs the chart, it injects the values into the template, generating the correct final YAML on the fly. This keeps configuration DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself).
lessons.instructions:
## Task: Accessing Values
Write the template syntax to inject the `replicaCount` from the values file.
lessons.starterCode:
spec:
  replicas: {{ .___.___ }}
lessons.solution:
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
lessons.hint: Use .Values.replicaCount
lessons.rubric: Correctly references .Values.replicaCount.

lessons.title: Custom Resource Definitions
lessons.theory:
## Extending Kubernetes (CRDs)
Out of the box, Kubernetes understands core resources like Pods (containers), Services (networking), and Deployments. But what if you want Kubernetes to understand something completely custom, like a 'DatabaseBackup' or a 'VideoRenderJob'?

You can extend the Kubernetes API by registering a **Custom Resource Definition (CRD)**. 

Once registered, you can write YAML files defining a `kind: DatabaseBackup` and send them to the Kubernetes API, and it will accept them just like native resources. This extensibility is why Kubernetes transformed from a simple container manager into a universal control plane that can manage external cloud resources, databases, and custom workflows.
lessons.instructions:
## Task: Define a CRD Group
Specify the `group` and `version` for a custom resource named `Database`.
lessons.starterCode:
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: databases.mabel.io
spec:
  group: ___
  versions:
    - name: ___
lessons.solution:
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: databases.mabel.io
spec:
  group: mabel.io
  versions:
    - name: v1
lessons.hint: Use mabel.io and v1
lessons.rubric: Correctly extracts the group from the name and sets version v1.

lessons.title: Reconciliation Loop
lessons.theory:
## The Control Loop
The core philosophy of Kubernetes is declarative state management, driven by the **Reconciliation Loop** (or Control Loop).

You do not give Kubernetes imperative commands (e.g., *'Start a new server'*). You give it a declarative state (e.g., *'There should be 3 servers running'*). 

The Reconciliation Loop constantly compares the **Desired State** (what you asked for in YAML) with the **Actual State** (what is physically running in the cluster). If you asked for 3 servers, and one crashes, the Actual State is now 2. The loop detects this drift and takes immediate action to 'reconcile' the difference by spinning up a new server. This loop runs endlessly, ensuring the system is self-healing.
lessons.instructions:
## Task: Return Result
In a Kubebuilder Reconcile function, return a successful empty result so the loop knows it finished correctly.
lessons.hint: Return empty struct {} and nil error
lessons.rubric: Correctly returns ctrl.Result{} and nil.

lessons.title: Traffic Shifting
lessons.theory:
## Safe Deployments in the Mesh
When deploying a new version of an API, immediately routing 100% of user traffic to the new code is incredibly risky. If there's a fatal bug, the entire system crashes for everyone.

A Service Mesh (like Istio) enables advanced deployment strategies like **Canary Releases** via Traffic Shifting. 

Because the Service Mesh proxy controls all network routing, you can configure it to route exactly 95% of traffic to the stable Version 1, and 5% of traffic to the new Version 2. You monitor the error rates on Version 2 for an hour. If it looks healthy, you shift the traffic to 50/50, and eventually 100%. If Version 2 throws errors, you instantly shift the routing back to Version 1 without any downtime.
lessons.instructions:
## Task: Virtual Service Weights
Configure an Istio VirtualService to send 90% of traffic to v1 and 10% to v2.
lessons.starterCode:
route:
- destination:
    host: my-service
    subset: v1
  weight: ___
- destination:
    host: my-service
    subset: v2
  weight: ___
lessons.solution:
route:
- destination:
    host: my-service
    subset: v1
  weight: 90
- destination:
    host: my-service
    subset: v2
  weight: 10
lessons.hint: Use 90 and 10
lessons.rubric: Correctly sets the weights to 90 and 10.

lessons.title: Mutual TLS (mTLS)
lessons.theory:
## Zero Trust Networking
In traditional legacy networks, perimeter security was the norm: build a strong firewall at the edge of the data center, but assume everything inside the network is safe and can talk to each other in plain text.

Modern cloud-native systems use a **Zero Trust** model. Even if a hacker breaches the firewall, they shouldn't be able to read the internal traffic between your microservices. 

A Service Mesh achieves this by enforcing **mTLS (Mutual TLS)**. When Service A talks to Service B, the sidecar proxies intercept the traffic, automatically verify cryptographic certificates on both ends (mutual authentication), and heavily encrypt the connection. This ensures that all internal microservice communication is fully encrypted and identity-verified, all without the developers having to write a single line of security code.
lessons.instructions:
## Task: PeerAuthentication

apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: default
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: ___
lessons.solution:
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: default
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT
lessons.hint: Use STRICT
lessons.rubric: Sets mTLS mode to STRICT.
